extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, public finance, and government policy (policymakers, historians, economists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria for how church organization and public revenue/expenditure ought to be structured; discusses effects of patronage, benefice size, methods of raising public revenue, and allocation of public expenses. Useful for assessing institutional arrangements in political economy and public finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episcopal government favourable to peace and good order
rubrics_metrics.description: “This system of church government was, from the beginning, favourable to peace and good order, and to submission to the civil sovereign.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that episcopal structures (sovereign disposal of bishoprics, established subordination among clergy) tend to stabilize society, promote loyalty, and avoid civil commotion. Example: Church of England valued for loyalty; anti-pattern is more popular election systems that generate faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign and lay patrons' right of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign (and other lay patrons) have the disposal or right of presentation to bishoprics and other consistorial benefices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formal right of presentation channels church appointments through patrons, concentrating influence with higher ranks. This arrangement fosters clergy alignment with sovereign/court interests and shapes clergy behavior toward patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical pursuit of patronage can neglect lower classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Clergy who curry favour with patrons by flattery, assentation, and cultivating elite arts are apt to neglect means of maintaining influence with the lower orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: clergy focused on pleasing nobility become ineffective with common people, failing to defend doctrines against popular enthusiasts. Positive behavior includes learning, decorum, good manners, social graces to earn elite esteem without abandoning parish duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular election of pastors tends to disorder and faction
rubrics_metrics.description: “As long as the people of each parish preserved the right of electing their own pastors, they acted almost always under the influence of the clergy, and generally of the most factious and fanatical of the order.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that open parish elections can empower factional clergy and fanatics, causing contests, schisms, and wider civic disturbance. Historical corrective: magistrates assumed presentation rights to preserve public peace (Scottish example; 10th of Queen Anne restored patronage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presbyterian equality among clergy (authority and benefice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presbyterian government establishes equality of ecclesiastical authority and (to a lesser extent) equality of benefice among the clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality of authority is usually perfect; equality of benefice less so. Where benefices are more equal, clergy are less tempted by patronage-seeking and tend to cultivate learning, regularity, and faithful duty—producing learned, independent, respectable clergy with influence among common people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of benefices encourages exemplary clergy and local influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where church benefices are nearly equal and moderate, clergy must rely on exemplary morals and modest living to gain respect, fostering stronger ties with common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediocrity of benefice forces clergy to behave in ways the populace respects (humility, assistance, respect for prejudices), increasing pastoral influence and broad conversion without persecution. Contrasts with large benefices that distance clergy from common people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of benefice distribution on universities and learned men
rubrics_metrics.description: Where benefices are moderate, a university chair is generally a better establishment than a church benefice; where benefices are considerable, the church drains universities of eminent men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains national differences: England’s rich church drains universities, while Geneva, Holland, Scotland (moderate benefices) have eminent professors. Implication for institutional design: benefit structures influence where intellectual talent congregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching obligation as method to render mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: “To impose upon any man the necessity of teaching, year after year, in any particular branch of science seems in reality to be the most effectual method for rendering him completely master of it himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: regular teaching forces review and correction of hasty opinions and deepens knowledge. Policy implication: public institutions that require teaching produce solid learning among men of letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church revenue is part of general state revenue and reduces resources for defence
rubrics_metrics.description: The revenue of every established church... is a branch... of the general revenue of the state, which is thus diverted to a purpose very different from the defence of the state. The more of this fund that is given to the church, the less... can be spared to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tithe acts like a land tax reducing landowners' capacity to contribute to defence; redistribution of public funds to church affects state readiness. Tradeoff: religious endowments vs. public/military expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper recompense should be proportioned to the nature of the service
rubrics_metrics.description: “The proper performance of every service seems to require, that its pay or recompence should be, as exactly as possible, proportioned to the nature of the service.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a service is underpaid → meanness and incapacity among those employed; overpaid → negligence and idleness. Example: overly rich clergyman loses time for duties and sanctity in eyes of common people. Principle for public pay-setting: align pay with expected service to incentivize competence and diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expenses for defence and sovereign dignity borne by general contribution proportionate to ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of defending the society, and that of supporting the dignity of the chief magistrate, are both laid out for the general benefit of the whole society... all the different members contributing, as nearly as possible, in proportion to their respective abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of distributive burden: general public goods should be funded collectively with contributions scaled to ability. Distinguishes between universal benefits (state defence, sovereign dignity) and more local or user-specific benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of justice can be funded by fees on those who occasion or benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The persons... who give occasion to this expense, are those who... make it necessary to seek redress or protection from the courts... The persons... most immediately benefited by this expense, are those whom the courts... restore or maintain in their rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice costs may be defrayed by court fees charged to litigants (those creating demand or benefiting). Exception: conviction of criminals with no estate may require general revenue. Allocation depends on practicality and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local or provincial expenses ought to be defrayed locally
rubrics_metrics.description: Those local or provincial expenses, of which the benefit is local or provincial... ought to be defrayed by a local or provincial revenue, and ought to be no burden upon the general revenue of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: police of a particular town/district. Justice: it is unjust that the whole society should contribute towards an expense whose benefit is confined to a part of the society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Road and communications funding: users may directly pay via tolls
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of maintaining good roads and communications is... beneficial to the whole society... The turnpike tolls in England, and the duties called peages in other countries, lay it altogether upon those two different sets of people [travelers and consumers], and thereby discharge the general revenue of the society from a very considerable burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, charge direct users or beneficiaries (carriers, consumers) to allocate costs efficiently and relieve general revenue. Tolls are an example of user charges aligning costs and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and religious instruction: beneficiaries or voluntary funding appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of the institutions for education and religious instruction, is likewise, no doubt, beneficial to the whole society... might, perhaps... be defrayed altogether by those who receive the immediate benefit... or by the voluntary contribution of those who think they have occasion for either the one or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple acceptable funding models: public funding, beneficiary payment, or voluntary support. Choice depends on distribution of benefits and feasibility of charging beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: General revenue must cover deficiencies when particular beneficiaries cannot
rubrics_metrics.description: When the institutions, or public works... either cannot be maintained altogether, or are not maintained altogether, by the contribution of such particular members... the deficiency must, in most cases, be made up by the general contribution of the whole society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: use specific or user funding first; if insufficient for socially beneficial works, top up from general revenue. Prepares transition to discussion of revenue sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of public revenue peculiarly belonging to sovereign: stock or land
rubrics_metrics.description: The funds, or sources, of revenue, which may peculiarly belong to the sovereign or commonwealth, must consist, either in stock, or in land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign-owned capital may be in tradable stock (managed/loaned for profit/interest) or land (rent). Each has different characteristics for stability and suitability as a permanent revenue source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue from stock: profit (active use) vs interest (lending)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign... may derive a revenue from [stock], either by employing it himself, or by lending it. His revenue is, in the one case, profit, in the other interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: profit from direct mercantile management (rare for states), interest from lending capital abroad or at home. Distinguish risk, management capacity, and return type when evaluating stock as public revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments generally poor managers of mercantile projects (except some cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: No two characters seem more inconsistent than those of trader and sovereign... The profusion with which the affairs of princes are always managed, renders it almost impossible that they should [succeed in trade].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical anti-examples: sovereign agents who are careless buy/sell at bad prices, overconsume resources, and mismanage trade (examples: English government vs East India Company, princes as merchants). Caveat: some aristocratic administrations (Venice, Amsterdam) managed mercantile projects competently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-office as an appropriate government mercantile project
rubrics_metrics.description: The post-office is properly a mercantile project... It is, perhaps, the only mercantile project which has been successfully managed by, I believe, every sort of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-office suitable because capital required is modest, business transparent, and returns are certain/immediate. Policy implication: governments can run certain service monopolies well when management is simple and predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock and credit are unstable/perishable for principal revenue; land is stable
rubrics_metrics.description: The unstable and perishable nature of stock and credit, however, renders them unfit to be trusted to as the principal funds of that sure, steady, and permanent revenue... Land is a fund of more stable and permanent nature; and the rent of public lands, accordingly, has been the principal source of the public revenue of many a great nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument for preferring land/rent as foundation for permanent public revenue (examples: ancient republics, crown lands). Stock-based revenue exposed to credit risk, war, and market changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lending public treasure and pawn-shop as revenue sources require security and peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The canton of Berne derives a considerable revenue by lending a part of its treasure to foreign states... The city of Hamburgh has established a sort of public pawn-shop... affords a revenue...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lending public capital yields returns but depends on (1) security of funds invested and (2) probability of continued peace. Pawn-shop yields steady local revenue. Risk assessment essential when using public treasure as income source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper bills of credit can be used to raise revenue but require demand, credit, and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: By advancing... paper bills of credit, to be redeemed fifteen years after their date... it raised a moderate revenue... The success... must have depended upon three different circumstances: first, upon the demand for some other instrument of commerce... secondly, upon the good credit of the government... and, thirdly, upon the moderation with which it was used...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy checklist for issuing paper credit as fiscal expedient: ensure market demand, strong governmental credit, and strict moderation in issuance. Misuse leads to disorder (American colonies example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantile projects may succeed under prudent, parsimonious administrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The orderly, vigilant, and parsimonious administration of such aristocracies as those of Venice and Amsterdam, is extremely proper... for the management of a mercantile project of this kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat to general rule that sovereigns are poor traders: well-managed, frugal, and disciplined administrations can profitably manage ventures (e.g., public bank, profitable projects). Success depends on institutional competence.
